_note: GH#397 Phase 2 work order. register/tag are a reproducible heuristic proposal plus recorded hand-audit overrides (classification-overrides.json). Region lanes may re-judge any string, but must log the change. `holdout` and `protected` rows are UNTOUCHABLE and are excluded from the queue by construction.

strings.text: The shopfront door, hung so it swings shut on its own. Past it, the market tier goes back to being civic.
She pushes a bowl of salted something across the counter at you without being asked, and takes the coin for it without apologising.
A broad Drake behind a counter worn pale in two places, one where the coins land and one where her elbow goes. Both are hers.
Twelve forms about one crate. You get four pages in before the words stop meaning anything.
The shop's own copy of every form the crate has generated, in a stack tall enough to stand a cup on.

[Appraise Goods] — Form nine, clause four: perishable household stock is exempt from queue hold. Tin is not perishable. The salt packed WITH it is, and it is on the same manifest line. Four cycles, and the exemption was on the paper the whole time.
Forms, in an order. There is a shape to the order. You cannot see the shape.
A cleared square of floor by the back wall with a chalk outline on it, the size of one crate, waiting since the first cycle.
The dock is squared away for today. Whatever else moves, it moves tomorrow.
You square the load onto the chalk outline. It fits the way a thing fits when somebody measured it a month ago and has been looking at the empty space since.
Third leg, last leg. The crate lands inside its own chalk outline and something in the back of the shop goes quiet, then very loud, then quiet again.
Jars in a rank, labels in a hand that got neater partway along the shelf and then went back to how it was.
Half the jars are from tiers you will never have a permit for. The keeper does not explain how, and you decide not to ask in a city this fond of paperwork.
A bench cut down to knee height, three sets of claw-marks along the front edge at three different heights.
Something small goes very still behind the bench, decides you are not interesting, and resumes an argument you cannot follow about whose turn it is.
The family's own board: who eats here on credit, and for how long. Names in chalk, never in ink.

strings.issue_named_work: issue-named button: two excellent specific sentences, then a third that tells the reader what to think about them
strings.text: Eleven names carried. One of them has been carried for two years and has no repayment column at all. In Pallass, that is a document nobody filed.
Nothing there. Jars from tiers you will never hold a permit for, dusted anyway.
Nothing there. Something small breathes behind the bench and decides to keep still.
A workbench of calipers, weights, and chalk lines — every tool squared to the bench edge. The Magus is up at the office when he is not down here.
Every tool squared to the bench edge. You decide against touching anything.
Bar stock stacked by gauge, each bundle strapped and tagged. The tags carry a tier number, a bench number, and nothing else. No names anywhere on them.
Cold iron, cut to length by somebody who measured twice. The strapping doesn't give under your hand.
A standing barrel of water beside the anvil, skinned over with scale and grey all the way down. The rim is worn smooth in the two places a smith's hands go.
The water is warmer than the room around it. Something went in here not long ago.
Cooled slag and cracked crucible shards, heaped no higher than a line painted on the flagstones around it. The line has been repainted recently, and brightly.
Glassy black waste, still holding a little of the day's heat. Even the refuse up here has a level marked on it.

A bronze rail along the tier's open edge, polished bright by a hundred people leaning on the same stretch of it while they waited on the cage. Below it the shaft goes down past where the light gives up.
You put a hand on the rail. Warm from the tier, not from the drop. Whoever set it worked out exactly how close a person could stand.
A rack of numbered slips beside the second bench: a stock number, a bench number, an hour. No names on any of them. Any pair of hands that can read a gauge can take one down.
The rack is empty until the next shift files its slips. Pallass does not run two shifts at once.
You take a slip, walk its stock number down to the racks and the finished piece back up. The clerk who pays you writes down the hour you took, to the quarter.
The smith hands you the slip before the rack does. She says nothing about it. She wouldn't.
A wide iron-strapped door standing open on its wedge. Past it: a working hall, and a heat that has its own weather.
A civic bin beside the second bench, half full of work that never left the tier. Each piece has a tag, and every tag has the same examiner's seal on it.
Nine blades in the bin, all from one hand, all failed on the same measure. Somebody up here is doing careful work and failing it the same way every time.
A slate of what the cage is carrying today, chalked by hour. Two lines have been rewritten so many times the slate has gone smooth under them.
One crate of tin, den shop, market tier. Logged three cycles running and carried none of them. Beside it, in a tidier hand: HELD, QUEUE.
A pallet strapped and tagged and standing exactly where it has stood for three cycles, one hand's width outside the loading square.
The pallet is where you left it and the cage is where the bell says. Nothing moves again until the next shift.
You get the pallet onto the loading square and the strapping squared. The attendant looks at it, looks at the bell, and says nothing, which is the whole permission you are going to get.
An anvil bolted to its own slab, a furnace mouth banked low beside it — cold for now, but built to run hot for a working day at a time.
The metal underfoot still holds the day's heat, hours after the last hammer fell.
A second bench, same pattern as the first — built to the same civic spec as the market tier's stalls, just built for heat instead of trade.
Tool racks, empty for the moment. Whoever works this bench keeps it orderly.
A bronze grate exhales a slow white breath, steady as a held note. Somewhere below, something enormous is always working.
Warm, damp air. A rhythm underneath it, too even to be weather.
The brass gate rises with a well-oiled clank, counterweights turning smooth in their track. The lift carries you down, into the ordered quiet of the market tier.
The brass gate is locked. A stencilled plate: PERMIT AND STAMP REQUIRED. The clerk's window is open.
A bronze-riveted cage, tall enough to swallow a wagon, counterweights racked in a shaft that drops past sight. This is how the tiers actually connect.
A stone shape stands too near the tier's own edge, cracks along its arms glowing a shade too bright for the forge-heat alone.
She sets the hammer down long enough to look at you properly. From her, that reads as a whole conversation.
A Drake in a scarred leather apron, forearms banded with old burn-marks she stopped covering years ago. She works without looking up, and the work doesn't suffer for it.
He tips two fingers off the gate lever. "Quarter bell," he says, which from him is a kindness and a schedule at once.
A Drake in a brass-buttoned lift coat, one hand resting on the gate lever without gripping it. He watches the counterweights instead of the passengers, and knows where both are.
Tongs, swages and fullers hung in size order along a painted rack, every one of them chalk-outlined on the boards behind it. An empty outline is a tool somebody still has.
You lift a set of tongs off its outline and set it back. Heavier than it looks, and it goes back exactly straight.
Every bench on the tier chalked in a column, the smith's mark beside it and the hours they're owed. Two marks have been rubbed out and rewritten in a different hand.
Bench hours, to the quarter. Nobody up here works a minute they can't account for.
Nothing there. Warm metal underfoot, and a rhythm below it that never quite stops.
Nothing there. Every tool on this tier is squared to an edge somebody measured.
The hall door, propped with a wedge nobody has ever removed. Past it, the tier's noise resumes.
Heat, metal, and a gauge you cannot read. Guessing here costs somebody a week.
A billet clamped mid-process, the quench beside it, a gauge nobody has reset since the last failure. Somebody stopped here on purpose and did not come back.
[Appraise Goods] — You read the grain off the colour, hold the count two beats longer than the slate says, and quench. The billet comes out with the standard's own answer in it.
Colour, count, quench. You can see there is an order to it. You cannot see the order.
A civic notice pinned at eye height, examiner's seal at the corner, the text underneath it read so often the ink has gone grey where thumbs land.
The standard does not measure how hard a blade comes out. It measures how it RECOVERS. Somebody up here has been failing the wrong test perfectly.
She looks up for exactly as long as the count allows, then back down. From an apprentice on the clock, that is a warm welcome.
A young Drake with her sleeves pinned back and a scorch on one forearm she has not stopped working long enough to notice.
Water gone grey with scale, a skin of oil across the top, and a scum line three fingers above the current level.
You touch the surface. Warm all the way down. This tub has not been cold in years, and the scum line says nobody has ever had time to change it.
A slate ruled into columns: heat, count, quench, result. The result column is chalked over so many times the surface has gone soft.
Forty-one attempts. Under the last one, in smaller writing than the rest: TRY THE OTHER WAY ROUND.
Finished pieces racked in a grid, each with a civic tag wired to it. They are not for sale. They are the argument.
Every piece on the wall passed. You count the tags: four different smiths, four different answers, one standard. Pallass framed the disagreement and hung it up.
The rig swings past its own marks and settles wrong, again and again. Whatever is out of true in it is the forge's business — until somebody on this floor makes it yours.
A squat rig on three legs, gauges banked along its front, correcting its own posture a half-beat after it needs to.
Nothing there. Quench water and hammer scale, under a wall of work that all passed.
Nothing there. The heat in here keeps a schedule, and you are not on it.

A squared plinth of the same slab the whole tier is cut from. No rune, no seam, nothing carved into it at all — and still the blankness has an outline, the way a mould does. Whatever door reaches this tier is already remembered here.
Cold, precise stone, and not as blank as it looks. Something the shape of a door is being held in it, patiently, for later.
State your business and your sponsor, or stand aside for the next in line.
Measure twice. I have measured everything in this hall at least three times, and I am still finding what I missed.
The brass gate rises with a well-oiled clank, counterweights turning smooth in their track. The lift carries you up, into noise and heat and orange light.
The brass gate is locked. A stencilled plate: PERMIT AND STAMP REQUIRED. The clerk's window is open.
A bronze-riveted cage, tall enough to swallow a wagon, counterweights racked in a shaft that drops past sight. This is how the tiers actually connect.
The rail, the drop, the haze. Pallass keeps its details above your pay grade.
[Eagle Eyes] — The haze gives up. Nine tiers resolve into stalls, patrol routes, and one dropped coin purse on a ledge two floors down that everyone else is too proud to see.
No more dropped coins by the railing today. Pallass sweeps on schedule.
Nine tiers of city below, if your eyes are good enough to spend on it.
Two grey shapes stand either side of an unclaimed stall, carved plating catching the tier's flat light, neither one moving.
Cunning Crafts! Best components on the tier, or the second-best, depending who is asking and how much they are buying.
A City Gnoll in a stained apron, shaggy fur tan under the stains, eyebrows singed down to stubble. He is arguing cheerfully with himself about the price of something.
You look like someone who could use a potion. Everyone can use a potion. Mine are only occasionally on fire — once.
A young human woman behind a fold-out consignment stall, talking fast, pricing three things at once and watching your hands to see which one you will pick up.
A working alchemist's bench, burners cold. You would not know where to start.
Cheap reagents racked by the burner, and a scorch-ring on the slate where a hundred crude workings went slightly wrong.
[Low-Grade Synthesis] — Crude reagents over a low flame, and a draught that mostly does what it should. It will pass.
Xif's spare bench, scrubbed and stocked. A low flame and a steady hand would turn it into something.
A glass drip-still, coiled and cold. The magic-water in it means nothing to you yet.
A coil of glass tubing over a low pan, magic-water beading down it one clarified drop at a time.
[Magic-Water Solvent] — The magic-water comes off the coil clear enough to bend the light. One phial, corked and ready.
A drip-still set for magic-water. Someone who knows the working could draw a clean solvent from it.
A bulb of dark glass over cold coals, half full of something grey. Not your trade.
A distilling retort, its bulb crusted white at the neck where the salts climb as the wash boils away.
[Mineral Distillation] — You boil the wash honest and slow. What is left is a spoonful of pale salts, the backbone of the next working.
A retort over a banked fire, a mineral wash already loaded. A distiller could boil it down to salts.
State your business and your sponsor. Everyone's business goes through this window eventually.
The good bench wants both halves of the working in hand: a solvent phial and a measure of mineral salts. You are short at least one.
The best bench Xif owns, kept for work you cannot do yet.
The bench Xif keeps for himself: clean glass, a steady blue burner, and room laid out for two reagents to become a third.
[True Synthesis] — Solvent into salts, in the one order that holds. What settles in the vial is clearer than either half went in.
The finest bench on the tier, and it knows it. A true synthesis needs solvent and salts both, and a hand that can bring them together.
The still wants a crude draught to work down. Your pack has nothing worth reducing.
A reduction still, hissing faintly. The valves mean nothing to you.
A copper still on a slow flame, built to boil a crude draught down to what it should have been the first time.
[Perfect Reduction] — The still takes the crude draught apart and returns only the part that matters, clear as morning.
Xif's reduction still, all coils and patience. In the right hands it turns crude work into clean.

Civic ordinances under glass, numbered and dated, the oldest one on the wall older than the wall. Nothing is pinned over anything else. There is a numbered slot for every notice and no notice without a slot.
Ordinances, numbered and glassed. Somewhere in Pallass a clerk owns the key to this case, and only that clerk.
Ordinance 44, third column: tier passes are the property of the city and the responsibility of the bearer. Yours is in your pocket, and now you know whose it is.

A weighing pillar set out where anyone can use it, brass pans hanging true, the city's own test weights chained to the column. Any stallkeeper's measure can be checked here against the city's, in front of everyone.
You set a hand on the pan and it swings back level. The chained weights have inspection dates stamped into them, the last one this month.
A shopfront wedged between two civic frontages, the only door on this row with a hand-painted sign and something cooking behind it.
A rank of low carts for hire, each chalked with a tier number and a rate, and a queue board nobody is standing at.
The rank is empty until the next rotation. Pallass hires carts on a schedule too.
You take a cart off the rank, walk the crate off the lift apron and across two blocks of very orderly stone, and nobody stops you once. The paperwork was never about the crate.
Second leg, same cart, same two blocks. The rank clerk marks it without looking up, which in Pallass is a commendation.
Empty crates stacked a head above the awnings behind the stalls. The razorbeak has decided they belong to the razorbeak, and no stallkeeper has argued yet.

It goes up off the crates and comes back screaming about the west end. The two standing things down there step aside for anyone whose permit is already filed — and the office that files it is the counter four stalls behind you.
Rows of chalked figures, precise to the copper, refreshed each morning by a clerk with steadier hands than yours. Nobody haggles here. Nobody needs to.
Chalk and slate. The numbers don't move for anyone.
A stall built to the same civic pattern as every other on this tier — same counter height, same awning pitch, same posted-price placard. Efficient. Impersonal.
Goods arranged in neat rows, prices chalked and unmoving. The stallkeeper barely looks up — the price is the price.
A stall built to the same civic pattern as every other on this tier — same counter height, same awning pitch, same posted-price placard. Efficient. Impersonal.
Goods arranged in neat rows, prices chalked and unmoving. The stallkeeper barely looks up — the price is the price.
A stall burner, hot and jealously watched. Renting it takes more than coin — it takes credentials.
[Advanced Cooking] — You cook on a stranger's fire in a city of critics, and the critics go quiet.
The stallkeeper's burner is free between rushes. Pallass argues about everything except good food.
A stall built to the same civic pattern as every other on this tier — same counter height, same awning pitch, same posted-price placard. Efficient. Impersonal.
Goods arranged in neat rows, prices chalked and unmoving. The stallkeeper barely looks up — the price is the price.
The price is on the board. It'll be the same price however long you stare at it.
A bronze grate exhales a slow white breath, steady as a held note. Somewhere below, something enormous is always working.
Warm, damp air. A rhythm underneath it, too even to be weather.
The window ledge is worn smooth where a thousand wrists have rested, waiting on a stamp. A stencilled plate lists the posted fees. Nobody argues with it.
Forms, inkwells, and a bell that has clearly been rung far too many times.
Nothing there. Chalked prices and swept stone, and not one thing outside its allotted square.
Nothing there. A clerk two stalls down writes something about you and moves on.
